stem: A 36-year-old woman at 32 weeks gestation in her fourth pregnancy has a known anterior placenta praevia overlying her previous lower segment caesarean section scar from 2 prior caesarean deliveries. Ultrasound at 28 weeks showed loss of the retroplacental clear zone, irregular lacunae within the placenta, and bridging vessels from the placenta into the bladder wall on colour Doppler. MRI has confirmed suspected placenta percreta with likely bladder involvement.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76 bpm, BP 118/70 mmHg, Temp 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Hb 116 g/L, group and hold current, no active bleeding

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Attempt vaginal delivery at 39 weeks with uterotonic agents on standby in case of postpartum haemorrhage from the praevia
options.rationale: Vaginal delivery is absolutely contraindicated with placenta praevia. Furthermore, placenta percreta with bladder involvement requires multidisciplinary planned caesarean delivery. Attempting vaginal delivery risks catastrophic haemorrhage and maternal death. (Source: RANZCOG - Placenta Accreta Spectrum)

options.text: Elective caesarean section at 39 weeks with attempted manual removal of the placenta at the time of delivery
options.rationale: Attempting manual removal of an accreta spectrum placenta is the single most dangerous action, as it disrupts the abnormal placental-myometrial-bladder interface and causes massive uncontrolled haemorrhage. The placenta must be left in situ. Additionally, delivery at 39 weeks is too late for confirmed percreta. (Source: RANZCOG - Placenta Accreta Spectrum)

options.text: Planned caesarean hysterectomy at 35-36 weeks at a tertiary centre with multidisciplinary team including urology and radiology
options.rationale: Confirmed placenta percreta with bladder involvement requires planned caesarean hysterectomy at a tertiary centre with a multidisciplinary team. Delivery is typically planned at 35-36 weeks to balance prematurity risk against the risk of emergency haemorrhage from unplanned labour or bleeding. The team should include senior obstetric surgeon, urologist (for bladder involvement), interventional radiologist (for potential internal iliac artery balloon occlusion), anaesthetist, neonatologist, and cell salvage/massive transfusion protocol. The placenta is left in situ and removed en bloc with the uterus. (Source: RANZCOG - Placenta Accreta Spectrum)

options.text: Elective caesarean at 37 weeks with placenta left in situ and methotrexate given postoperatively for placental resorption
options.rationale: Conservative management (leaving the placenta in situ without hysterectomy) may be considered in accreta or increta where the patient strongly desires uterine preservation, but it is not appropriate for percreta with bladder involvement. The risk of secondary haemorrhage, sepsis, and delayed hysterectomy is very high. Methotrexate has not been shown to reliably promote placental resorption and risks immunosuppression. (Source: RANZCOG - Placenta Accreta Spectrum)

options.text: Admit now for uterine artery embolisation to devascularise the placental bed before planned delivery at 38 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Pre-delivery uterine artery embolisation is not standard practice for placenta accreta spectrum. Interventional radiology may place internal iliac artery balloon catheters preoperatively to assist with haemostasis during caesarean hysterectomy, but embolisation prior to delivery risks placental ischaemia and fetal compromise. (Source: RANZCOG - Placenta Accreta Spectrum)

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) disorders encompass accreta (adheres to myometrium), increta (invades myometrium), and percreta (penetrates through myometrium into adjacent organs). Risk factors include previous caesarean section (strongest risk factor - exponentially increasing with number of prior caesareans), placenta praevia overlying a previous scar, and prior uterine surgery. Planned caesarean hysterectomy at a tertiary centre at 35-36 weeks is the standard of care for percreta. Attempting placental removal is the most dangerous action and must be avoided. The multidisciplinary team approach has significantly reduced maternal mortality from this condition.
key_points: Never attempt manual removal of an accreta spectrum placenta - leave in situ and proceed to hysterectomy
Delivery at 35-36 weeks balances prematurity risk against emergency haemorrhage risk
Multidisciplinary team is essential - obstetrics, urology, interventional radiology, anaesthesia, haematology
The risk of PAS increases exponentially with number of prior caesarean deliveries
explanation.pearls: After 3 prior caesarean deliveries with a concurrent anterior placenta praevia, the risk of placenta accreta spectrum exceeds 60% - this combination should trigger early referral to a PAS-experienced tertiary centre.

sources.label: FIGO - Placenta Accreta Diagnosis and Management
RCOG - Placenta Praevia and Accreta Green-top Guideline

stem: You are the obstetric registrar on call. A midwife calls urgently from the birth suite. A 28-year-old woman at 37 weeks gestation with a singleton pregnancy had spontaneous rupture of membranes 5 minutes ago. On vaginal examination, the midwife palpated a pulsating cord loop below the presenting part. The fetal head is at minus 2 station. The CTG shows acute fetal bradycardia at 80 bpm. Cervical dilatation is 5 cm.

data_table.Examination: Cervix 5 cm dilated, cephalic at -2 station, pulsating cord below presenting part, membranes ruptured, liquor clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Manually elevate the presenting part off the cord, fill the bladder with 500 mL warm saline, and expedite category 1 caesarean section
options.rationale: Manual elevation of the presenting part is correct as the first action and bladder filling to maintain elevation is an appropriate adjunct. However, the critical missing step is positioning the patient in the knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg position, which is the most immediately effective action to relieve cord compression alongside manual elevation. (Source: RANZCOG - Cord Prolapse)

options.text: Commence IV oxytocin augmentation to expedite vaginal delivery as the cervix is already 5 cm dilated with active labour
options.rationale: At 5 cm dilatation with the presenting part at minus 2 station, vaginal delivery is not imminent and cannot be expedited safely in the timeframe required to prevent fetal hypoxic brain injury. Cord prolapse with sustained bradycardia requires delivery within 30 minutes. Emergency caesarean section is the appropriate mode of delivery. (Source: RANZCOG - Cord Prolapse)

options.text: Attempt to replace the cord above the presenting part and apply a fetal scalp electrode for continuous heart rate monitoring
options.rationale: Cord replacement (funic reduction) is not recommended as it is rarely successful, risks cord spasm and vessel damage, and delays definitive management. The cord should be kept warm and moist but not handled excessively. The focus must be on relieving cord compression and expediting delivery. (Source: RANZCOG - Cord Prolapse)

options.text: Administer terbutaline 250 mcg subcutaneously to stop contractions and wait for the cord pulsation to improve and normalise
options.rationale: Tocolysis with terbutaline may be considered as an adjunct to reduce uterine contractions contributing to cord compression while preparing for emergency caesarean section. However, it is not a definitive treatment and must not delay surgical delivery. Waiting for the CTG to normalise before proceeding would unacceptably delay delivery. (Source: RANZCOG - Cord Prolapse)

options.text: Place the patient in steep Trendelenburg or knee-chest position, manually elevate the presenting part, and call for category 1 caesarean
options.rationale: The immediate priorities in cord prolapse are to relieve compression on the cord and expedite delivery. Positioning in steep Trendelenburg or knee-chest uses gravity to lift the presenting part off the cord. Continuous manual elevation of the presenting part via vaginal examination maintains this relief. Category 1 (emergency) caesarean section is called with a target decision-to-delivery interval of under 30 minutes. Retrograde bladder filling with 500-750 mL saline can maintain elevation during transfer to theatre. The cord should be kept warm and moist, and minimal handling is important to prevent vasospasm. (Source: RANZCOG - Cord Prolapse)

explanation.summary: Cord prolapse is an obstetric emergency with a risk of fetal hypoxia and death if not managed rapidly. The immediate management triad is: position (steep Trendelenburg or knee-chest), elevate (manually lift the presenting part off the cord), and deliver (emergency caesarean section unless vaginal delivery is imminent). Retrograde bladder filling with 500-750 mL warm saline via Foley catheter can maintain upward displacement of the presenting part during transfer to theatre. Risk factors include malpresentation, polyhydramnios, preterm gestation, artificial rupture of membranes with a high presenting part, and multiparity.
key_points: Knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg positioning is the most immediately effective action to relieve cord compression
Manual elevation of the presenting part must be maintained continuously until delivery
Category 1 caesarean section with decision-to-delivery time under 30 minutes is the target
Retrograde bladder filling with 500-750 mL saline can maintain presenting part elevation during transfer
explanation.pearls: Cord prolapse occurs most commonly with artificial rupture of membranes when the presenting part is not well applied to the cervix - always confirm the presenting part is well engaged before amniotomy, and never perform amniotomy with a high mobile head.

sources.label: RCOG - Umbilical Cord Prolapse Green-top Guideline

stem: A 33-year-old primigravida at 35 weeks gestation presents with worsening frontal headache and visual blurring over the past 12 hours. Her pregnancy has been complicated by gestational hypertension diagnosed at 31 weeks. She reports increasing upper abdominal discomfort and nausea today. Fetal movements remain present. On review of antenatal records, fetal growth was on the 12th percentile at the most recent ultrasound. In the assessment unit she appears uncomfortable and photophobic. Reflexes are brisk. CTG demonstrates a reactive trace without decelerations.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 174/112 mmHg, HR 96 bpm, RR 20/min, Temp 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Brisk reflexes with 2-beat clonus, right upper quadrant tenderness, mild pedal oedema
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 108 x10^9/L, ALT 96 U/L, creatinine 102 micromol/L, urine protein:creatinine ratio elevated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Increase oral antihypertensive therapy and continue expectant management because CTG remains reassuring
options.rationale: Oral antihypertensives plus expectancy is wrong because severe pre-eclampsia features (neurological symptoms, severe BP, thrombocytopenia, transaminitis) need IV control plus magnesium and delivery planning; oral escalation is inadequate. Would be correct only for mild gestational hypertension without severe features (SOMANZ Hypertension Guideline).

options.text: Commence magnesium sulfate and plan expedited delivery after maternal stabilisation
options.rationale: Severe pre-eclampsia with neurological symptoms and end-organ involvement requires seizure prophylaxis and delivery planning after stabilisation. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension Guideline)

options.text: Administer corticosteroids and delay delivery for at least 7 days because prematurity risk outweighs maternal concerns
options.rationale: Steroids and delay 7 days is wrong because at 35 weeks maternal severe disease outweighs prematurity considerations; the anti-pattern is treating maternal severe disease as a trade-off for fetal lung maturity at near-term gestations. Would be correct only at earlier preterm gestations with stable maternal status (RANZCOG Hypertensive Disorders).

options.text: Arrange outpatient blood pressure review tomorrow because fetal wellbeing remains reassuring
options.rationale: Outpatient review tomorrow is wrong because severe pre-eclampsia features mandate inpatient management with magnesium sulfate; the anti-pattern is using fetal wellbeing alone to justify outpatient care. Would never be correct with severe features (SOMANZ Hypertension Guideline).

options.text: Commence intravenous antibiotics because thrombocytopenia and transaminitis suggest occult sepsis
options.rationale: IV antibiotics for sepsis is wrong because the pattern (HELLP-like with neurological symptoms and severe BP) supports severe pre-eclampsia, not sepsis; thrombocytopenia and transaminitis fit HELLP. Would be correct only with clinical or microbiological evidence of infection (RANZCOG Hypertensive Disorders).

explanation.summary: This patient has severe pre-eclampsia with neurological symptoms, severe hypertension, thrombocytopenia, liver involvement, and renal impairment. Maternal stabilisation with magnesium sulfate and planning for delivery are required despite reassuring fetal monitoring. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension Guideline)
key_points: Reassuring CTG does not negate severe maternal disease. (Source: RANZCOG Hypertensive Disorders)
Magnesium sulfate reduces eclampsia risk in severe pre-eclampsia. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension Guideline)
explanation.pearls: Right upper quadrant pain in pre-eclampsia may reflect hepatic involvement and impending severe complications. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension Guideline)

subtopic_detail: Amniotic fluid embolism recognition and management
stem: A 35-year-old woman, gravida 3 para 2, is undergoing induction of labour at 40 weeks gestation with an oxytocin infusion. Shortly after artificial rupture of membranes, she develops sudden onset of severe dyspnoea, agitation, and rapidly progressive cyanosis. Within 2 minutes she becomes unresponsive. The CTG shows a sudden prolonged fetal bradycardia. Her partner reports she appeared well seconds before the collapse.

data_table.Vital signs: BP unrecordable, HR 140 bpm (sinus tachycardia), SpO2 75% on high-flow O2, RR 36/min, GCS 3
data_table.Examination: Cyanotic, unresponsive, profuse dark vaginal bleeding beginning after collapse, no signs of placental abruption noted on prior assessment

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and critical initial management?

options.text: Massive pulmonary embolism - commence IV heparin and arrange CT pulmonary angiogram
options.rationale: While massive PE can cause sudden cardiovascular collapse in pregnancy, the timing immediately after ARM, the rapid onset of coagulopathy (evidenced by profuse haemorrhage), and the fetal bradycardia in a labouring patient are more consistent with amniotic fluid embolism. PE typically does not cause immediate DIC. CT angiography is not feasible in a peri-arrest patient. (Source: RANZCOG Safety Communique: AFE; ACEM Emergency Obstetrics Guidelines)

options.text: Placental abruption - IV fluid resuscitation and expedite vaginal delivery
options.rationale: Placental abruption can cause haemorrhage and fetal bradycardia but does not typically present with sudden cyanosis, SpO2 of 75%, and cardiovascular collapse preceding the haemorrhage. In abruption the bleeding usually precedes or coincides with the collapse, whereas in AFE the cardiovascular collapse occurs first followed by DIC and haemorrhage. (Source: RANZCOG Safety Communique: AFE)

options.text: Amniotic fluid embolism - activate MET, perimortem caesarean within 4 minutes, and manage DIC
options.rationale: The sudden onset of cardiovascular collapse with profound hypoxia immediately after ARM, followed by DIC (coagulopathic haemorrhage) and fetal bradycardia, is the classic presentation of amniotic fluid embolism. Management is: (1) activate the medical emergency team, (2) commence CPR if pulseless, (3) perform perimortem caesarean section within 4 minutes of cardiac arrest to relieve aortocaval compression and improve maternal resuscitation, (4) aggressive management of DIC with blood products (packed red cells, FFP, cryoprecipitate, platelets), (5) inotropic support. There is no specific treatment for AFE; management is supportive. (Source: RANZCOG Safety Communique: AFE; ACEM Emergency Obstetrics Guidelines; ANZCOR Guideline 14.1)

options.text: Eclamptic seizure - IV magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose and left lateral position
options.rationale: Eclampsia presents with generalised tonic-clonic seizures, not with sudden cyanosis and cardiovascular collapse without seizure activity. There is no mention of seizure, hypertension, or proteinuria. The profound hypoxia and DIC are not features of eclampsia. (Source: RANZCOG Pre-eclampsia Guideline)

options.text: Anaphylaxis to oxytocin - cease infusion, IM adrenaline 500 mcg, IV fluids
options.rationale: While anaphylaxis to oxytocin is possible, it is extremely rare and would present with urticaria, bronchospasm, and hypotension rather than the triad of sudden cardiovascular collapse, respiratory failure, and coagulopathy seen in AFE. The coagulopathic haemorrhage is a distinguishing feature of AFE not seen in anaphylaxis. (Source: ASCIA Anaphylaxis Guidelines; RANZCOG Safety Communique: AFE)

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare but catastrophic obstetric emergency with a mortality rate of 20 to 60%. The classic presentation involves sudden cardiovascular collapse (Phase 1: right heart failure and pulmonary vasospasm) followed by coagulopathy and haemorrhage (Phase 2: DIC and left ventricular failure). The trigger is often artificial rupture of membranes, intrauterine manipulation, or high-amplitude contractions. Diagnosis is clinical as there is no confirmatory test in the acute setting. Management is entirely supportive: aggressive resuscitation, perimortem caesarean section within 4 minutes if cardiac arrest occurs, massive transfusion for DIC, and inotropic support.
key_points: Classic triad: sudden cardiovascular collapse, respiratory failure, and coagulopathy
Perimortem caesarean section within 4 minutes of cardiac arrest improves maternal survival
No specific treatment exists - management is entirely supportive
DIC develops rapidly and requires aggressive blood product replacement
explanation.pearls: AFE is the leading cause of direct maternal death in Australia; the diagnosis should be considered in any labouring woman who develops sudden unexplained cardiovascular collapse, particularly if coagulopathic bleeding follows within minutes.

stem: A 28-year-old primigravida with a monochorionic diamniotic (MCDA) twin pregnancy is noted to have discordant amniotic fluid volumes at her 20-week scan. The donor twin has a maximum vertical pocket (MVP) of 1.5 cm with a collapsed-appearing bladder, while the recipient twin has an MVP of 12 cm with a distended bladder. The recipient twin has an absent a-wave on ductus venosus Doppler. Umbilical artery Doppler in both twins shows present end-diastolic flow. No hydrops is observed in either twin.

data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound 20 weeks MCDA twins: Donor twin MVP 1.5 cm, bladder not visualised. Recipient twin MVP 12 cm, distended bladder. Recipient DV absent a-wave. UA Doppler: present end-diastolic flow both twins. No hydrops. EFW discordance 18%

lead_in: What Quintero stage is this and what is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Quintero stage I - serial ultrasound surveillance every 2 weeks
options.rationale: Quintero stage I is defined by oligohydramnios-polyhydramnios sequence (MVP below 2 cm in donor, above 8 cm in recipient) WITHOUT absent donor bladder. In this case, the donor bladder is not visualised, which advances the staging to at least stage II. Stage I may be managed with surveillance, but this patient has progressed beyond stage I. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy Guideline; Quintero Classification TTTS)

options.text: Quintero stage II - amnioreduction of the recipient sac to relieve pressure
options.rationale: While this could be classified as stage II (oligo-poly with absent donor bladder) if the Doppler were normal, the abnormal ductus venosus waveform in the recipient (absent a-wave) advances this to stage III. Amnioreduction is a temporising measure that reduces polyhydramnios volume but does not address the underlying placental vascular anastomosis causing TTTS. Fetoscopic laser ablation is the treatment of choice for stage II and above at 16 to 26 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy Guideline; Eurofetus Trial)

options.text: Quintero stage IV - urgent delivery by caesarean section at tertiary centre
options.rationale: Quintero stage IV is defined by hydrops in either twin. This case does not demonstrate hydrops, so stage IV is not reached. Stage V is intrauterine death of one or both twins. Urgent delivery at 20 weeks is not viable. The appropriate management for stage III at 20 weeks is fetoscopic laser ablation, not delivery. (Source: Quintero Classification TTTS; RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Quintero stage III - referral for fetoscopic laser ablation of placental anastomoses
options.rationale: This presentation meets Quintero stage III criteria: oligo-polyhydramnios sequence (MVP 1.5 cm donor, 12 cm recipient), absent donor bladder (stage II), PLUS abnormal Doppler (absent a-wave in recipient ductus venosus, which is a stage III criterion). The Eurofetus trial demonstrated that fetoscopic laser ablation of communicating placental anastomoses is superior to serial amnioreduction for TTTS stage II and above at 16 to 26 weeks, with higher survival rates and lower neurological morbidity. Referral to a tertiary fetal medicine centre with laser capability is the appropriate management. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy Guideline; Eurofetus Trial; Quintero Classification TTTS)

options.text: Quintero stage III - selective fetal reduction of the recipient twin
options.rationale: Selective fetal reduction (cord occlusion) in MCDA twins is reserved for situations where laser ablation is not feasible or has failed, or when one twin has a lethal anomaly threatening the co-twin. At Quintero stage III at 20 weeks with both twins alive, fetoscopic laser ablation is the first-line intervention. Selective reduction sacrifices one twin and is not the primary approach. (Source: RANZCOG Multiple Pregnancy Guideline; Fetal Medicine Foundation TTTS Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome affects approximately 10 to 15% of monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancies. It results from unbalanced blood flow through placental vascular anastomoses. The Quintero staging system classifies severity: Stage I (oligo-poly only), Stage II (absent donor bladder), Stage III (abnormal Doppler), Stage IV (hydrops), Stage V (demise). The Eurofetus randomised trial established fetoscopic laser ablation of communicating anastomoses as the standard treatment for TTTS stage II and above at 16 to 26 weeks, achieving at least one survivor in approximately 76% of cases compared with 56% with amnioreduction.
key_points: Quintero staging: I=oligo-poly, II=absent bladder, III=abnormal Doppler, IV=hydrops, V=demise
Fetoscopic laser ablation is the treatment of choice for stage II+ at 16 to 26 weeks
The Eurofetus trial showed laser ablation superior to amnioreduction for survival
Abnormal ductus venosus Doppler (absent or reversed a-wave) defines stage III
explanation.pearls: In the Quintero classification, the abnormal Doppler criterion for stage III includes absent or reversed end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery, reversed flow in the ductus venosus, OR pulsatile flow in the umbilical vein in either twin; the presence of any one of these in the context of stage II findings advances to stage III.
